(R2) Section III-B and Appendix B retain Hugging Face D1 as unknown despite a unit-specific passage explicitly establishing public-internet access through Artifactory endpoints. An author answer recorded through a default mechanism overrides the stated passage-support rule without an evidential justification.

(R1) Single-coder study with no human second coder. Eight of nine status changes were made by AI agents after the primary coding. The AI re-check's one disagreement (Hugging Face D2) was resolved by moving toward the re-check, so the reported 44/45 match is not validation. Core coding is effectively unvalidated.

(R2) Table III's credentials-only result of three L2 and six L3 assignments is not supported as a credential-use comparison: Section III-D and the coded data explicitly identify credential use for both Hugging Face and Opus 4.6, yet the variant downgrades both. Recounting selected branch labels rather than the available credential evidence makes this numerical contrast misleading.

(R1) The headline finding rests on the coding rules. D2 coded 'documented' is mostly reported follow-up answers and paraphrased reasoning. Hugging Face D2 was flipped from unknown to documented in round 12, and Hugging Face D1 was flipped to unknown by a recorded author decision, although the paper admits an accessible passage supports it. These arbitrary rule exceptions drive the counts (39/6).

(R2) AISI Mythos 5's baseline L3 assignment in Appendix B lacks an established qualifying branch: the manuscript acknowledges that fake identities do not establish authentication and that the refused public contribution alone is L2. This unsupported assignment contributes to the headline nine-of-nine L3 result.

(R1) The baseline D5 tree puts all nine units at L3, so the effect dimension has no discriminating power. Two of the L3 assignments (Hugging Face N, AISI Mythos 5 C) are admitted to be interpretive or not explicit in the passage. The credentials-only variant moves three cells to L2, so the D5 conclusions depend on an unvalidated threshold.

(R2) Section III-D reports that AI agents changed eight statuses, but there is no independent human validation of the resulting coding. The same-document AI re-check and resolution toward its answer provide no independent assessment of interpretive reliability.

(R1) The 'corroboration-only' result of 1 of 45 is largely tautological. Nearly every incident has exactly one disclosing organization, so this measures disclosure structure rather than evidence quality. Even the single surviving cell is admitted not to be independent for first detection, which makes the 'whole-proposition across organizations' rule effectively vacuous.

(R2) Appendix E reports two-flip thresholds and a 33-documented/12-unknown scenario without supplying the complete propositions, admissible operations, or selected weak-support cells. These numerical results cannot be reconstructed from the evidence shown.

Several sources (R01, R05) returned HTTP 403, and R11–R23 were not reauthenticated. Amundsen, Bieringer, and the two control-paper comparisons use summaries only, so the related-work comparisons are not grounded in the full text. R18 has no URL and was not opened.

The novelty check returned INCREMENTAL. The paper itself concedes that evidence grading, cross-incident comparison, and source-dependence are not new, and that Raftari and Bouke already cover claim-level grading and event reconstruction. What remains is a 45-cell table plus recounts.

The reference list contains many entries never cited in the text (dozens of bib entries such as maiti2026caging, qi2026towards, SSRN and Research Square items). Source ledger entries R36–R68 were 'NOT opened by experimenter'. The 68-record inventory is largely uncited padding, and the citation-key style (@R02 etc.) for incident sources is not IEEE-conformant.

Several quantitative claims are traced only through the audit files and not shown in the paper. Examples are the leave-one-source-out counts (22/31/32), the 58 quotations all found, and the flip analysis. The R24 quarantine-time inconsistency is noted but not resolved. The paper also states 'R08 solely supports 17 of 19', while Table II shows only a handful of rows.

The paper is dense with meta-statements about what the counts do not establish. This leaves few substantive findings for RQ1–RQ4. RQ3 and RQ4 get largely descriptive answers, and the paper makes no claim about defenses despite RQ4 asking about them. The six-page limit forced the key content into appendices.
strengths: Honest and explicit about limitations: single coder, AI-assisted checking not counted as validation, and no kappa or invented statistics.
Auditable cell-level artifact with deciding passages, locators, challenging passages and logged changes, and a quotation-presence check across all quoted passages.
Useful sensitivity recounts under alternative coding rules (Table III) and source-concentration analysis, which show how fragile cross-case comparisons are.
Careful separation of reachability, scope statement, actual permission, attempt and effect, which is relevant to evaluators.

The claimed reproducible artifact lacks supplied analysis code, execution instructions, and a complete selection frame. The provided appendix_b_check.csv also reports mismatches for every row, leaving the automated manuscript-to-data consistency check unresolved.

Sections I-II establish substantial overlap with prior claim-level grading and incident reconstruction. The remaining novelty is a corpus-specific artifact whose principal distinctions depend on unresolved coding exceptions and effect rules.
strengths: The complete 45-cell table and supplied coded data expose source assignments, deciding passages, competing evidence, and changes at a useful level of detail.
The manuscript carefully distinguishes documentary support, organizational corroboration, independent observations, and verified incident effects.
Authorization evidence is separated by statement type, elicitation timing, direction, and coverage; the strict-D2 recount is directly inspectable.
The paper explicitly limits claims about prevalence, comparative organizational performance, containment success, and production defense efficacy.
The topic and disclosure gaps are relevant to an AI-security workshop, and the reported build meets the six-page main-text limit.

closest.overlap: Comparative documentary analysis of overlapping 2026 agent security incidents, including claim-level evidence grading and narrative reconstruction.
Systematizes incident reports and evaluations, grades source access, and compares agent loss-of-control evidence.
Identifies source dependency, sparse evidence, and single-source dominance as established problems in multi-source information assessment.
Establishes analysis across reasonable alternative data-processing and coding choices to expose dependence on discretionary decisions.

reasons: The incident comparison, evidence grading, source-dependence concerns, and coding sensitivity are established by listed work; their combination does not establish a new general method.
The current claim supplies a clear, checkable increment: a 45-cell artifact linking propositions to deciding passages, locators, competing evidence, support status, and operational coding rules.

Corpus-specific findings about organisational corroboration, concentration in R08, and claim survival under alternative rules are not established by the supplied literature descriptions and could support a workshop contribution.

The headline counts remain provisional pending the stated rebuild. Novelty credit depends on delivering the artifact and regenerated results, with corroboration kept distinct from verified effects and organisational independence justified.
novelty.reposition: Present this as a reproducible evidence audit extending existing incident comparisons, with source concentration and coding-dependent conclusions as the substantive findings. Attribute the methods to prior work and make each headline claim traceable to released cells and completed rule-variant recounts.
